title: Attorney General of Kansas

context.text: Neither primary was contested on August 4, 2026. The race repeats 2022, which Kobach won by about 15,800 votes (1.6 percentage points).
The Kansas Reflector's primary-night report and The Green Papers list only Kobach (R) and Mann (D) for Attorney General.

candidates.name: Kris Kobach
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced unopposed from the August 4 Republican primary.

summary.text: Kris Kobach is Kansas's Republican Attorney General, seeking a second term. He served as Kansas Secretary of State from 2011 to 2019 and has been Attorney General since 2023; his campaign emphasizes lower crime rates, a fentanyl task force, and lawsuits against federal policy.

background.text: Earned a bachelor's degree from Harvard University, a graduate degree from Oxford University and a law degree from Yale University.
Clerked on the Tenth Circuit, taught constitutional law at the University of Missouri at Kansas City, and was counsel to U.S. Attorney General John Ashcroft.
Kansas Secretary of State 2011-2019; Attorney General since 2023.

priorities.text: Continue the crackdown on fentanyl: at the October 6 debate he called it his top second-term priority.
Law enforcement: his campaign cites the lowest Kansas crime rate in 57 years and endorsements from 51 sheriffs.
Persuade more cities and counties to enter agreements with federal agencies to enforce immigration law (the Kansas Reflector's account of his debate remarks).

statements.quote: sued and stopped the Biden Administration from allowing biological males in girls’ locker rooms and on girls’ sports teams.
statements.context: From his campaign website's list of achievements as Attorney General.

statements.quote: A lot of it has to do with how we’ve used the KBI and also how we’ve removed violent illegal aliens who are allowed to remain in Kansas.
statements.context: On why Kansas's crime rate has fallen, at the October 6 Johnson County Bar Association debate.

record.text: Testified before a U.S. House Judiciary subcommittee on birthright citizenship on September 2, 2026, calling the Supreme Court's June decision upholding birthright citizenship 'weakly reasoned' and urging Congress to legislate on birth tourism.
A Shawnee County judge sanctioned him and his solicitor general $1 for filing a motion in a court lacking jurisdiction in the driver's-license gender-marker case he brought in 2023.
A Kansas district judge dismissed his lawsuit seeking to force Gov. Laura Kelly's administration to turn over SNAP recipient data to the federal government.

candidates.researchNotes: The Kansas AG's website blocked automated access, so official press releases were not used; record items come from Kansas Reflector reporting. Quotes and the transgender-sports line are from his campaign site. His immigration remarks are shown as a statement, not a position, because the Reflector paraphrases his stance and only one clause is a direct quote.

candidates.name: Chris Mann
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced unopposed from the August 4 Democratic primary; endorsed by the Kansas State Lodge of the Fraternal Order of Police.

summary.text: Chris Mann is the Democratic nominee for Attorney General and Kobach's 2022 opponent. A Lawrence attorney, he was a police officer until a drunk driver struck him during a 2002 traffic stop, then a Wyandotte County prosecutor and a Kansas Securities Commission attorney.

background.text: Became a police officer at 21; was struck by a drunk driver during a traffic stop in 2002, ending his law-enforcement career.

Attended Washburn University School of Law on a Koch Public Service Scholarship, then was an Assistant District Attorney in Wyandotte County and a Senior Staff Attorney at the Kansas Securities Commission.
Runs a private practice representing victims of drunk-driving crashes.

priorities.text: Return the office to public safety basics and ensure local law enforcement and prosecutors have the resources they need.
Fight fraud and scams, using his Securities Commission experience.
Address domestic violence cases with partners across the state.

candidates.researchNotes: Not an officeholder, so no record. On the death penalty he said it is the Legislature's role to set policy and that he would prosecute capital cases (Kansas Reflector); this does not map to an issue statement in the guide.
